title: There and back
description: Rebuild a page from its Markdown twin and see what the trip kept, what it dropped, and which converter bugs it caught.
bodyHtml:
There and back

Every page on this site has a Markdown twin for agents, and the build writes most of them by pressing the HTML down with html-to-md.ts. This page runs the other direction. It takes a twin, rebuilds HTML from it with a 250-line parser, and shows what came home. On 2026-10-13 I ran all 60 twins through the trip, and it found five bugs in the converter that writes them, all fixed in #1309.

Take a page on the trip

Pick a page. Your browser fetches the page and its twin from this site, rebuilds the twin as HTML with md-to-html.js, and counts what each leg kept.

enable JavaScript to run the trip

The test is a fixed point

A twin is written in a small language: headings, paragraphs, lists, quotes, code fences, tables, links, images and three kinds of emphasis. If the parser reads that language exactly, then pressing its output down again has to hand back the same twin, byte for byte. That gives the trip a pass condition, and either converter can fail it.

Of the 47 twins the build writes from pages in src/pages/, this one included, all 47 now come back byte for byte. Before the fixes below, 43 did. The 13 hand-written twins in src/content/md/ each settle after one trip, and every change is one of form: an autolink like <https://…> comes back as a bracketed link, a table rule gains spaces, and a fence loses its json label because the generator never writes one. No hand twin lost a word.

What the trip caught

The trip carries two checks, and between them they found five bugs in the converter that writes twins. Each read like ordinary text, so a person reading the twin would not notice, and every agent that read one got it.

The fixed point failed on four twins, and three of those failures were one bug. The escaper treated any text run that started like a list marker as the start of a line, even mid-sentence. On /garage/horizon and /lwe/fhe that wrote \+, which Markdown reads back as a plus sign. On /garage/octane it wrote Next.js \16., and a backslash before a digit is not an escape, so readers saw the backslash. The fourth failure was on /garage/wire, where a line break inside a table cell became three spaces.

The word count catches what the fixed point cannot, because a twin that already lost something still closes. /garage/wire and /garage/workers each lost a table caption, 197 words on wire, because the table renderer walked the rows and never visited <caption>. /garage/iroh read QUIChole-punching, because the converter dropped a text node that held only a space, and that one bug fused 33 pairs of words across 17 pages. The /lwe heading read **Learning With Errors**explaining, because its CSS sets the tagline apart as a block and the heading path never asked.

The trip also caught my first fix. Keeping that lone space made the homepage twin read 2026  · You, where an HTML comment split two runs of whitespace, and the fixed point failed on it before the fix shipped.

What never makes the trip

Across those 47 pages the HTML weighs 2.6 MB. The twins weigh 749 KB, and the rebuilt HTML weighs 839 KB. The difference is the part of a page that does something: 202 scripts, 362 buttons, 69 form controls, 21 canvases and 58 style blocks. The converter drops all of them on purpose, because a button's label without its behavior would read to an agent as a claim.

The words come through. Against the page's own reading text, the rebuilt HTML keeps every word on 45 of the 47 pages. The other two lose only superscripts: 2^n three times on /lwe/dac and 2^256 on /lwe/lean.

Two marks cannot come back. A superscript becomes ^2 and a subscript becomes _2, and neither has a closing mark, so the parser cannot tell them from a caret or an underscore in prose. It leaves both as text.

editorial.reader: Someone who serves Markdown twins to agents and trusts the converter because the twins look right.
editorial.problem: The reader checks a twin by reading it, and a converter bug that drops a caption or fuses two words reads fine, so nothing they check can see it.
editorial.thesis: An inverse parser turns the twin language into a fixed point that the converter can fail, and with a word count against the page it found five converter bugs that every twin hid by reading like ordinary text.
evidence: On 2026-10-13, 43 of 47 generated twins came back byte for byte after HTML to Markdown to HTML to Markdown, and all 47 did after the fixes in #1309.

The four failures traced to html-to-md.ts: a mid-line list escape on three pages, visible as a stray backslash on /garage/octane, and a line break flattened in a table cell on /garage/wire. The word count found dropped table captions on /garage/wire and /garage/workers, a lost space that fused 33 pairs of words across 17 pages, and a heading that ran its tagline into its title on /lwe.
The demo fetches a page and its twin from this site and recounts the trip in the reader's browser.
editorial.uncertainty: The parser reads only the language this site's converter writes, so a twin from anywhere else may not close, and superscripts and subscripts cannot round trip at all.

understanding.intro: Before you close the hood, check the mechanism in three questions.

questions.q: Why does pressing the rebuilt HTML down again test the converter at all?

options.t: If the parser reads the twin language exactly, a second pass has to return the same twin, so any difference is a bug in one direction.
options.why: Right. The fixed point gives the trip a pass condition that both converters can fail.

options.t: Because the rebuilt HTML matches the original page byte for byte.
options.why: It cannot. The trip drops every script, button and style block on purpose, so the HTML is always smaller.

options.t: Because a Markdown file that renders without errors is correct.
options.why: Every twin rendered fine, including the ones with bugs. Rendering cannot see a dropped caption.

questions.q: Which twin failure would point at the inverse parser instead of the forward converter?

options.t: A construct the generator writes that the parser reads back as something else.
options.why: Right. That breaks the fixed point on the parser's side, which is what the dl and line-break fixes during this build were.

options.t: A table caption missing from the twin before the trip starts.
options.why: The caption was already gone from the twin, so the forward converter lost it.

options.t: A hand-written twin whose autolinks come back as bracketed links.
options.why: That is a change of form with no change of meaning, and the trip settles after it.

questions.q: What would you predict for a page whose content is all canvases and buttons?

options.t: A short twin, a small rebuilt page, and most of the HTML bytes left behind on the way down.
options.why: Right. The converter keeps the prose around a demo and drops the demo, so the twin holds only the words.

options.t: A twin that describes each button so an agent can press it.
options.why: The converter drops controls on purpose, because a label without its behavior would read as a claim.

options.t: A failed trip, because the parser cannot rebuild a canvas.
options.why: The canvas never reaches the twin, so the parser never sees it. The trip can still close.
